newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Macquarie says any buy-back would be modest.
newsitem.headline: Macquarie says any buy-back would be modest.

text.p: Maquarie Bank Ltd managing director Allan Moss said on Wednesday that any capital return considered by the investment bank would be modest.
"Shareholders should not expect a large return in capital," Moss told reporters after the bank's annual meeting.
"There may not be any return in capital at all, but if there is one it will be modest," Moss said.
Moss would not detail how large a modest capital return would be.

Earlier, Macquarie Chairman David Clarke told the meeting the Reserve Bank's new capital adequacy standards for market risk to apply from January 1 would increase Macquarie's tier one capital adequacy ratio to about 13 percent from the 10.7 percent ratio as of March 31, 1997.
This was well above the Reserve Bank's minimum level of four percent.

Clarke said Macquarie was analysing its capital situation, but added that it was unlikely any capital return would involve a major reduction in capital as Macquarie's strong capital position made it flexible and ensured counterparty confidence.
Moss said ratings agencies had told Macquarie they would be comfortable with a tier one ratio of about nine percent.
"But, having a very strong capital base does give us a lot commercial flexibility and of course the bank has been producing a very high return on equity of about 25 percent after tax," Moss said.
"It's not clear that we should be taking steps to reduce that capital ratio. We'll be considering that issue over the course of the year," he said.
Moss would not say what would be an optimal level of capital to have.
"If there is one (a capital return), it will be modest because we've got a very fast-growing business here," Moss said.

Newspapers have reported in recent days that Macquarie was considering a share buy-back or other form of capital returns to absorb A$150 million of excess capital and reduce its tier one capital adequacy ratio to about nine percent.
"I do not think that the issue of a share buy-back will be a material factor for our stock," Moss said.
Earlier, Macquarie's annual meeting approved a proposal to change its articles of association to allow Macquarie to make preference share issues.
Moss said Macquarie had no plans to raise capital through preference share issues and the change had no effects on its capital management plans.
"It would be quite erroneous to read any strategic implications into the preference share amendments," he said.
Moss also repeated earlier comments from Clarke that Macquarie's mortgage securitisation arm PUMA would not increase significantly its profit contribution in the current year.
Moss said Macquarie was investing heavily in systems to improve service to clients. This investment was being expensed within the year, affecting the profit contribution.

"As a result of that very substantial investment in service delivery, we're not expecting profits from PUMA will increase materially this year, but we're very, very confident that volumes will continue to grow," he said.
Profits from PUMA would grow in later years, he said.
Moss said he would not elaborate further on Clarke's earlier comment that the first quarter results were well ahead of the same quarter a year earlier.
He said it was too early to forecast the full year results.
Macquarie's reported a A$116.94 million net profit in the year to March 31, 1997, up 25.4 percent from 1995/96.

Macquarie's shares had risen 20 cents to A$13.25 by 1.05 p.m. (0305 GMT), after earlier hitting an all-time high at A$13.40. Macquarie's shares have now risen over 60 percent from their 1997 low of A$8.22 on March 12.
Macquarie shares listed on the Australian Stock Exchange on July 29 at an initial price of A$6.95.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
